newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina calls newsman's death attack on democracy.
newsitem.headline: Argentina calls newsman's death attack on democracy.

text.p: Argentine authorities on Tuesday condemned the killing of a news photographer found shot and burned in a car this weekend as an attack on democracy and a throw-back to the death squads of the 1970s.

"It is a direct attack on journalism, a harsh message that takes us back to the sad times of the 1970s ... and was meant to destabilise our democratic system," Buenos Aires Province Gov. Eduardo Duhalde said as he tripled to $300,000 the reward for information about the attack he called "mafia-style."

Noticias news magazine photographer Jose Luis Cabezas was buried on Tuesday after a 24-hour wake attended by hundreds of Argentine news photograhers wearing black mourning ribbons. They later gathered around Buenos Aires' landmark obelisk and clapped hands in a symbolic act of repudiation.

His killing has sparked outrage across South and North America at an act that was a reminder of thousands of death squad killings before and after the coup of 1976 that left Argentina with a military regime that lasted until 1983.

"This murder recalls the terrible methods of the Triple A," said Argentina's independent Permanent Assembly for Human Rights, referring to the feared right-wing paramilitary death squad that operated in Argentina in the 1970s.

When police found Cabezas' body on Saturday in a ditch by a dirt road outside the beach resort of Pinamar, southeast of Buenos Aires, it was so badly burned it was only identified by his car keys and watch. He was handcuffed and had been shot in the head and his body doused with fuel and set on fire.

Cabezas, 35, was covering the summer season in Pinamar, the favourite resort of politicans and business leaders. He had also recently covered high-profile corruption cases, including revelations of crime syndicates in the Buenos Aires police.

Noticias, Argentina's top-selling weekly news magazine, is critical of the Peronist government of President Carlos Menem and last year caused the firing of one of his ministers by revealing a murky neo-Nazi past.
Menem voiced his "total condemnation of this savage act" at a news conference on Monday and promised his government "will not rest until the culprits are found."
Cabezas' colleagues have avoided adding to speculation about the motives. His boss, Carlos Lunghi, said Cabezas "was not investigating any story that could cause conflict."
